annotations.title: Summarize worst, median and best outcomes

description: Reports one outcome's worst, median and best cases from one run of a model. By default, worst is the lowest value in any trial, median is the middle value, and best is the highest value. The labels name the lowest and highest values, which suits an outcome where higher is better, such as revenue. For a cost or a duration, where lower is better, the scenario labelled worst is the cheapest or fastest case, so describe it to the user as the best case, and the one labelled best as the worst case. You can ask for other percentiles instead, such as the 10th and 90th, or the 80th for a P80 total. Use this when you want a short worst, typical and best case story. For the range or the odds of outcomes (what range it could land in, how likely something is), use run_monte_carlo_simulation instead; to find which input matters most, use rank_inputs_by_impact. It takes the model inline in graph, or a saved model by graph_id directly, so you do not need get_graph first, and you can call it on a saved model that may be unfinished: if an input in the saved graph has no distribution yet, the call is refused with incomplete_model, which names every such input and costs nothing. It returns each scenario's outcome value and every input's own value at the same percentile of that input's distribution. Those input values are an estimate, not the exact inputs of that trial. It also returns a run_id; a long run comes back as status running, and get_simulation_results gives you progress and then the result. Cost: one run per call. Without an account, 1 of your 3 free runs per UTC day, for a model up to 1,000 trials and 20 nodes; that daily allowance is counted per network address and client, so on a shared platform such as Claude.ai or ChatGPT you may find today's free runs already spent by someone else. Signed in with a free Kromatic account, 1 of 10 free runs per UTC day, for a small model (trials x nodes x periods at most 100,000, and within 10,000 trials and 50 nodes), spent before any credits. Beyond that -- a larger model, or a day whose free runs are used up -- 1 credit for a small run or 5 for a large one (a large run is any run over 100,000 trials x nodes x periods), currently $0.50 per credit; buy_credits tops up. A model that is invalid, or over the limits of the tier you are in, is rejected before running and costs nothing. A run that starts and then fails mid-run is refunded only where something can be given back: credits are not charged, and a signed-in free run goes back into today's allowance, but a free run without an account is not refunded and stays counted for the day.

graph.description: The model: root_nodes (uncertain inputs), calc_nodes (formulas), edges (links; formulas refer to them like {e1}) and run_params (trials and time periods). Same format as run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph, which documents formulas, periods, distributions and financial metrics in full. Give this or graph_id, not both. Only this outline is published here: the full schema is on run_monte_carlo_simulation's graph parameter, and the neumann://catalog resource lists every distribution and formula function. Neumann checks the model against that full schema when you call this tool and names any problem.

graph_id.description: The id of a graph you already saved, to analyse that graph instead of sending it inline. Give this or graph, not both. Requires a Neumann account -- an anonymous caller must use graph instead. If an input in the saved graph has no distribution yet, the call is refused with incomplete_model, which lists those inputs. The refusal costs nothing (no credit or free run is spent and no run is recorded), so there is no need to check your balance: give each one a distribution, save the graph again under the same id, and try again.
graph_id.title: Graph Id

percentiles.description: A list of percentiles of the outcome to report. Each is a fraction from 0 to 1: 0.1 is the 10th percentile, the value 10% of trials fall below. Default [0, 0.5, 1]: 0 is the lowest trial (labelled worst), 0.5 the median, and 1 the highest trial (labelled best). Other values are labelled like p10 (10th percentile). Values between 0 and 1 are estimated from a histogram. The labels assume higher is better: for a cost or a duration, 'worst' is the lowest (cheapest or fastest) trial, so ask for percentiles such as 0.1 and 0.9 and read them as low and high.
percentiles.title: Percentiles

seed.description: Optional whole number that fixes the random draws, so repeating the call gives the same result. Exact repeats are guaranteed only for small runs, where trials × nodes × time periods is at most 100,000.
seed.title: Seed

target_node_id.description: The id of the outcome node to measure. Defaults to the last calc node in the model, which is usually the final outcome.
target_node_id.title: Target Node Id

time_period.description: Index of the time period to measure, counting from 0: with 12 monthly periods, 11 is month 12. Defaults to the last period. This measures the node's value in that one period, not a total. For a cumulative figure such as year-one profit, add a running-total calc node with formula {e1} + {e2}, where e1 brings in the per-period value and e2 is an edge from the running-total node to itself with delay 1. Then target that node at index 11. This delayed self-edge is allowed; only loops with no delay are errors. In run_monte_carlo_simulation, use a cumsum metric instead.
time_period.title: Time Period
